body.text: Attribution: Krishna Vohra and Manish Vaidya, “The Ecological Cost of AI,” ORF Special Report No. 330, Observer Research Foundation, November 2026.

In just over a decade, the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) has attracted unprecedented levels of investments, with more than US$1.3 trillion invested since 2013.[1] In 2025, the Stargate Project announced by United States (US) President Donald Trump pledged up to US$500 billion for the construction of AI-focused data centres and computing infrastructure.[2] Much of this capital has flowed to leading tech firms that shape the bulk of AI innovation, such as Nvidia, OpenAI, Meta, and Oracle,

Big Tech has emerged as the principal force behind the rapid advancement of the AI industry, which can safely be described as an oligopoly, comprising a small group of firms with concentrated market power, a combined market capitalisation exceeding US$20 trillion,[3] policy influence, and close institutional embeddedness.[4],[5] Their influence has become further pronounced as they gain proximity to political power.[a]

Champions of AI expansion point to both the economic returns and societal benefits of AI. For example, PwC estimates that AI could add up to US$15.7 trillion to the global economy by 2030,[6] boosting global GDP by around 14 percent through gains in productivity, innovation, decision-making, and human–capital complementarity.[7] In addition to the direct applicative benefits of AI, the expansion of AI infrastructure is expected to generate wider spillovers through agglomeration effects, including knowledge diffusion, local employment creation, and multiplier effects.[8] At the same time, the costs of failing to adopt AI are becoming increasingly significant for firms: from rising operational inefficiencies and diminished competitiveness to slower innovation and weaker productivity growth.

The proliferation of AI has also been accompanied by claims about its potential to address climate change by accelerating scientific research and optimising energy systems. In practice, however, the applications that have driven the bulk of this investment, including large language models (LLMs), AI-generated images and video, and general-purpose chatbots, offer no meaningful climate benefit. What they do require, in substantial and growing quantities, is energy, water, and hardware.

Despite how AI tools are marketed, it is not magic powered by an immaterial force in the cloud. Every AI prompt is sent to a data centre, which requires massive amounts of energy to operate and clean water for cooling. The training and usage of AI relies on an extensive network of data centres; these are physical facilities that house IT infrastructure such as servers, storage systems, and networking equipment, with racks and rows of computers containing specialised Graphics Processing Units (GPUs).[9] This infrastructure is highly resource-intensive, driving substantial increases in electricity consumption, water use, and demand for critical materials. As AI adoption accelerates, questions surrounding environmental sustainability are becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

This report focuses on the resources used by AI and data centres in an era of scarcity as well as the byproducts created, such as emissions and e-waste, that together cause harm to the environment and weaken the case for AI’s benefit in the fight against climate change.

This discussion is highly relevant for India as data centre expansion is being treated as an unambiguous national priority. Prime Minister Narendra Modi, speaking ahead of the AI Impact Summit in New Delhi in February 2026, declared, “We invite the whole world’s data to reside in India.”[10] Excluding China, the Global South accounts for over 50 percent of the world’s internet users[11]—meaning they generate huge amounts of data—yet the US alone accounts for 44 percent of global data centre power capacity.[12] This asymmetry has driven legitimate ambitions around data sovereignty and domestic infrastructure investment across the developing world. Many, however, argue that expanding data centre infrastructure, primarily to support AI development, is not the solution to this asymmetry and could create more problems than it solves.

In a data centre, electricity consumption is distributed across five key components—namely, storage systems, networking equipment (such as switches), cooling systems, batteries and power supply units, and other auxiliary uses (such as lighting). The proliferation of AI is expected to markedly increase energy demand, as the scale of data centre infrastructure expands and the adoption of AI accelerates, with projected electricity demand outpacing global electricity growth rate averages (see Figure 1).

At the same time, data centre-related emissions have skyrocketed since 2022 (see Figure 2). In 2025, AI-related emissions were equivalent to the annual aggregate emissions of New York City and more than 8 percent of the aggregate global aviation emissions.[14] While targets by Big Tech firms estimate a flattening and subsequent decline in their carbon footprint, these remain mere projections without guaranteed emissions reduction. Moreover, even when accounting for these declines, the levels remain concerning, especially at a time when multiple climate tipping points and decarbonisation targets have already been breached.

In the context of data centres, emissions are generally classified into three categories: Scope 1, Scope 2, and Scope 3 emissions. Scope 1 covers direct emissions generated from on-site sources, such as backup diesel generators, cooling equipment, and other localised operational processes. Scope 2 are indirect emissions from purchased electricity used to power AI infrastructure, including servers, cooling systems, and computational workloads. Scope 3 captures broader value chain impacts, including emissions associated with semiconductor manufacturing, hardware production, construction of data centre infrastructure, logistics, and end-of-life e-waste disposal.[16]

While all three scopes are relevant for assessing the environmental footprint of AI, Scope 2 emissions are central to understanding and managing the ecological impact of AI data centres. Scope 1 emissions are limited due to the highly electrified nature of AI infrastructure, and Scope 3 emissions remain distributed across complex global supply chains. Scope 2 emissions constitute the dominant share of AI’s carbon footprint. The continuous large-scale electricity input required to power the infrastructure results in disproportionately high indirect emissions, since a substantial share of grid electricity in many countries continues to be generated from fossil fuels, particularly coal and natural gas.[17] Moreover, the scale of electricity demand generated by AI places considerable pressure on national and regional power grids, often necessitating additional fossil fuel-based generation capacity to meet rising demand.

Accelerating demand for AI-driven applications is driving the expansion of energy footprint of data centres. In regions where electricity generation remains fossil fuel intensive, this surge translates directly into higher carbon emissions. Estimates by the International Energy Agency (IEA) suggest that under a baseline scenario, global electricity demand from data centres could grow by around 15 percent annually between 2024 and 2030,[18] with the aggregate demand driven by the entire tech sector rising by as much as 60 percent by 2030, relative to 2020 levels (see Figure 2).[19] This is reflected in the carbon footprints of leading technology companies such as Alphabet, Amazon, and Microsoft, whose indirect emissions have increased by up to 150 percent over the past three years.[20] This trajectory reinforces concerns about the environmental sustainability of AI-led growth, underscoring the urgent need to align digital expansion with clean energy sources, improve data centre efficiency, and ensure optimal location choice for data centres.

There are currently close to 9,000 data centres worldwide, a figure expected to triple by 2030.[21] The US remains the global leader, followed by Europe and key economies in Asia-Pacific.[22] Efficient data centre operation is tied to geography. Facilities are ideally located in cooler climates to reduce the need for energy-intensive cooling systems. However, a growing share of capacity is being deployed in warmer regions, where cooling requirements are significantly higher and less environmentally efficient, increasing both electricity consumption and emissions intensity.

Moreover, while data centre infrastructure is currently concentrated in advanced economies, where relatively stronger regulatory frameworks and proactive energy transition policies help mitigate environmental impact (see Table 1), this is likely to change as AI adoption accelerates in emerging economies such as India and the Philippines. Data centre expansion in these regions—characterised by higher temperatures, grid instability, and lack of universal electricity access—will make the energy imperative far more urgent.

The impact of data centre expansion is also highly heterogeneous across countries. According to the IEA, data centres could account for up to 50 percent of electricity demand growth in Japan by 2030, compared to around 24 percent in other advanced economies and just 5 percent in emerging and developing economies.[24] These differences reflect variations in energy systems, resource endowments, policy environments, and fiscal capacity. Ensuring that new capacity is aligned with renewable energy adoption, grid resilience and sustainability goals will be critical to managing the environmental footprint of the global digital economy.

A second critical variable in the environmental management of data centres is water consumption. These facilities house server architectures that generate immense heat as a byproduct of continuously processing large volumes of data. Water is required to prevent overheating.

There are two principal cooling methods: (a) evaporative cooling systems, where water circulates through pipes, absorbs heat from servers, and is released as steam outside the facility; and (b) closed-loop systems, where the heated water is cooled using chillers and recirculated within the system.[27] The former is considerably more water-intensive, as it requires a continuous supply of fresh water.

A medium-sized data centre can consume up to 110 million gallons of water annually, with daily usage reaching several million gallons of potable water. For instance, Google has reported consuming over 6 billion gallons of water across its data centre operations in a single year.[28]

At the micro level, individual user choices incur a tangible water footprint. Estimates from the Omni Calculator AI Footprint,[29] suggest that running just 10 searches on ChatGPT is equivalent to using 138 litres of water. When scaled across annual usage and millions of users, the activity compounds dramatically: ten searches per user is comparable to filling up to 27,600 Olympic-sized swimming pools.[30]

A recent example of this compounding consumption can be observed in Ashburn in Virginia, United States—often referred to as the “data centre capital of the world”. The high concentration of hyperscale data centres in the region has placed massive pressure on local electricity grids, water resources, and public infrastructure.[31] In 2023 alone, data centres across Northern Virginia consumed nearly two billion gallons of water.[32]

The ecological implications of AI-driven water demand are thus difficult to ignore as the technology scales and supply is redirected from critical uses such as irrigation, drinking, and sanitation. The impact is amplified in water-stressed regions, where competing demands on limited resources are already acute. Five aspects merit attention:

Location: Data centre siting has historically prioritised cost, political feasibility, and agglomeration benefits over environmental sustainability. As a result, many facilities operate in already water-stressed regions, such as Arizona and Nevada in the US,[33] and Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Greater Noida in India.[34] These regions are characterised by declining groundwater reserves, where potable water is increasingly diverted towards industrial use, often at the expense of poor local communities.[35] Location choice must therefore be treated as a strategic environmental decision.

Opportunity cost: The use of clean drinking water for AI in an era of scarcity creates a zero-sum conflict with essential needs such as agricultural irrigation, public sanitation, and domestic drinking water. While AI promises productivity gains and complements human capital, prioritising industrial consumption over basic human and developmental needs is both economically and ethically indefensible. Data centres must therefore be viewed as a secondary use, contingent on first meeting basic human needs.

Lack of transparency: Underreporting and transparency gaps persist. Much like emissions accounting, water consumption by data centres is often selectively disclosed,[36] leading to systematic underreporting. This obscures the true environmental footprint of AI infrastructure, limits accountability, and undermines effective policy responses.

State subsidies: Regulatory frameworks frequently distort market incentives by supplying water to large technology firms at rates significantly below true economic value. For example, data from operations in Texas suggests that tech firms avail of heavily discounted rates instead of paying the full cost of water provision.[37] Such pricing gaps fail to reflect the scarcity value of water resources.

Ecological disruptions: In addition to absolute volume extraction, water-intensive cooling processes create ecological and thermal disruptions. Evaporation, discharge, and thermal pollution can affect local ecosystems, disrupt flora and fauna, and exacerbate environmental stress. These, in turn, create long-term ecological imbalances that must be factored into the assessment of AI’s environmental footprint.

There is an urgent need for stronger economic and societal accountability for Big Tech firms. The adverse impacts of rising water demand must be internalised through appropriate incentives, regulatory frameworks, and pricing mechanisms, thus encouraging both greater investment in safer, environmentally sustainable cooling alternatives and a more optimal mix of water-based and non-water-based solutions, such as natural and immersion cooling.[c]

A third dimension of the impact of data centres—one that has received even less scrutiny—is the generation of massive volumes of e-waste and hardware detritus. Since current waste management systems are not equipped to handle e-waste at this scale, large amounts of e-waste end up in landfills or are incinerated, severely compromising air and water quality at disposal sites.[38]

UN Global E-Waste Monitor (ITU/UNITAR) reported 62 million tonnes of e-waste generated in 2022, containing an estimated US$91 billion worth of critical metals including copper, gold, and silver.[39] However, less than a quarter of the e-waste generated was recycled, with only 1 percent of global rare-earth element demand met through e-waste recovery.[40] This loss is amplified by the exceptionally short commercial lifespan of AI infrastructure. For example, GPUs and servers are replaced every one to five years, as successive model generations render previous ones commercially obsolete. New research estimates that generative-AI alone could create up to five million metric tonnes of accumulated e-waste by 2030.[41] Countries restricted from accessing advanced chips generate up to 14 percent more e-waste per unit of computing output.[42] Thus, redirecting these finite raw materials—obtained through ecologically harmful extraction and mining—from critical green technology to a short-lived AI hardware pipeline not only incurs a steep opportunity cost but also accelerates global material loss.

Furthermore, when hazardous e-waste is improperly managed—such as via open burning or incineration in waste-to-energy plants—the emissions release harmful heavy metals and other pollutants into the atmosphere. Similarly, when e-waste ends up in landfills, material such as lithium batteries can combust and increase the incidence of landfill fires, which are challenging to extinguish.

In India, for example, this hardware detritus adds to a pre-existing waste management crisis. Research from the Mandoli industrial area in Delhi has found heavy metal concentrations in groundwater from informal e-waste recycling sites exceeding both Indian official standards and the World Health Organization’s (WHO) permissible limits for drinking water.[43] Components without resale value are openly burnt or dumped, releasing dioxins, PM10, and heavy-metal particulates into the air and water of communities already contending with coal-fired power and over-extracted groundwater.[44] In FY 2023-24, India generated 175,000 metric tonnes of e-waste, with formal processing capacity already insufficient to absorb it.[45] A 2026 CPCB assessment found 17 states and union territories with no registered recycling facilities.[46] Waste that the formal system cannot absorb passes to the informal sector, exacerbating soil and water degradation.

Addressing the e-waste challenge requires regulatory interventions that discourage early hardware replacement cycles—this requires political intent rather than technological breakthroughs. In India, for example, the 2026 Union Budget proposed a tax holiday up to 2047 for foreign companies providing cloud services through Indian data centres,[47] effectively removing the fiscal leverage required for the government to enforce responsible infrastructure practices. Similarly, EPR compliance under the E-Waste (Management) Rules 2022,[48] verified recycling partnerships, and regional facility requirements that close the 17-state gap should not be voluntary addenda to investment deals. There should be conditions attached to such arrangements, and taxation should not be abolished for an industry that poses these risks without guarantees of compliance.

Ultimately, improving downstream recycling capacity offers limited relief due to the structural barriers inherent in e-waste processing.[49] Electronics are rarely designed with recyclability in mind, and the economics of proper recycling and recovery seldom work in its favour. As India invites the world to build the digital infrastructure of the Global South, replicating the extractive model of the countries that built the first generation of this infrastructure and inheriting their waste alongside their workloads, will not result in data sovereignty. The AI bubble may be short-lived, but the debris it generates will endure for generations.

Big Tech firms exercise control over the critical inputs underpinning AI development—including data, talent, computing infrastructure, and financial capital—while also serving as first movers in the development and deployment of these technologies. This concentration of economic and technological power places Big Tech at the centre of the emerging AI ecosystem. As a result, these firms not only shape the pace and direction of AI innovation but also influence the broader social, economic, and environmental externalities associated with its expansion. Their decisions therefore play a defining role in determining both the future trajectory of AI and its wider societal and environmental consequences.

A key area of concern is how Big Tech addresses its environmental footprint, specifically the mechanisms through which firms mitigate the externalities arising from their operations and broader value chains. The environmental management toolkit available to these firms can be classified into four categories: (a) accounting, measurement, and compliance frameworks; (b) market-based instruments; (c) operational and efficiency-oriented tools, including abatement technologies; and (d) AI-driven solutions. From an economic perspective, these interventions largely operate on the supply side,[50] aiming to reduce emissions intensity, improve resource efficiency, and manage the climate impact of digital infrastructure expansion. In practice, firms often deploy a combination of these instruments.

Big Tech’s climate mitigation measures largely centre on ambitious commitments, polished reporting mechanisms, clean energy procurement, and market-based offsets. Only 26 percent of all climate claims made by these companies are supported by cited research, while 36 percent lack substantiation and the remainder rely on questionable estimates.[51] Furthermore, claims regarding climate goals, emissions reduction, and the AI–climate improvement nexus have largely been premised on traditional AI, which has a relatively lower ecological footprint compared to modern, rapidly expanding, and consumer-facing generative-AI systems.

Thus, Big Tech’s environmental strategy relies on managing rather than mitigating its environmental impact through creative accounting[d] and elements of greenwashing. These firms are increasingly viewed as prioritising perception management and signalling over tangible, measurable, and verifiable environmental outcomes. As the ecological strain of AI intensifies, many companies are doubling down on greenwashing tactics.[e],[52]

Furthermore, the framing of AI as a primary mitigator of climate change remains highly questionable. Most modern AI-based applications, particularly consumer-facing generative systems, are far from being environmentally benign. As highlighted at the AI Impact Summit in Delhi,[53] the technology sector increasingly presents carbon-intensive infrastructure and climate solutions as a bundled narrative, often conflating traditional, lower-intensity AI with the far more energy-intensive generative-AI ecosystem.

Looking ahead, a critical challenge lies in designing incentive mechanisms for Big Tech firms to move from signalling to tangible, verifiable environmental action. While the technology–growth nexus is well established, the technology–environment relationship warrants greater scrutiny. Much of the current discourse is characterised by regulatory noise and perception management. At the same time, the oligopolistic nature of the industry has implications for both environmental policy discourse and the prioritisation of climate goals.

These dynamics are further influenced by exogenous factors such as the political environment, lobbying, and intra-industry competition. Passive measures, such as accounting-based emissions reductions and participation in carbon markets, are thus insufficient. They must be accompanied by active and tangible investments in abatement technologies, as well as strategic and legally binding location selection frameworks for data centres that account for regional environmental constraints.

There is growing concern among digital communities about the ecological tax of unchecked AI growth. The internet, particularly social media platforms and messaging apps, are flooded with low-utility, high-volume AI-generated content—often referred to as “AI slop”—ranging from automated text overviews to synthetic audio and generative imagery. This saturation has led many environmentally conscious users to boycott specific apps entirely.

However, individual boycott is not sustainable, since many of these apps have become embedded in people’s daily lives. This is complicated by the fact that most platforms routinely embed generative features directly into core user interfaces, without providing opt-out mechanisms. For example, every Google search automatically generates an AI overview above search results and messaging apps now have chatbots built into core functions. Resources are being used at concerning rates, leading to rising emissions and more e-waste generation—all without the consent or knowledge of those using the platform.

Raising awareness about the ecological consequences of AI use is a necessary first step. Using AI responsibly requires using it less, and actionable user strategies must prioritise structural reduction.

• Unnecessary uses of AI, including the excessive uses of LLMs to outsource mundane everyday tasks, must be reduced. Every request that is not sent to a data centre, directly conserves energy and water while reducing emissions.
• Generating images and videos—far more resource-intensive than text-based queries—for online trends must be avoided.
• Greater transparency must be demanded for AI tools and their impact on emissions, energy demands, and water usage, as well as user-controlled toggles to disable automated inference features.

However, while civic advocacy and consumer usage reduction are necessary preconditions for systemic change, the burden of ecological stabilisation must not be shifted entirely onto user behaviour. First, a shift in user behaviour is fundamentally limited since platforms often impose AI within their user interface without giving opt-out options. Moreover, a significant share of the ecological impact of AI occurs long before deployment: immense volumes of energy and water are consumed in the training of each new model, frequently rushed to the market despite the lack of genuine demand. Similarly, automatic integration of AI tools and features into everyday functions causes a rise in emissions that users have no control over.

On the development side, sustainable scaling requires clear prioritisation of use cases that are both climate-conscious and beneficial to end users. Machine learning models can offer clear utility when used for solving challenges such as precision agriculture, climate prediction, and grid optimisation. However, most investment is currently being channelled into low-value consumer-facing models such as chatbots or image generators. These use cases are neither economically profitable nor environmentally sustainable, and their unfettered advancement can be ecologically disastrous without any direct benefit to solving the climate crisis. Tech conglomerates cannot credibly position AI as a tool for climate action while using fossil fuel-based data centres to power an expansion focused on low-utility use cases.

Advocates for the environment and experts in the field call for ensuring ecological sustainability and ethical resource management before continuing rapid data centre expansion. For AI to responsibly contribute to climate mitigation, its advancement must be powered by renewable energy and prevented from exacerbating water scarcity. While regulators are struggling to keep pace with the speed of AI and data centre development, governments do not lack precedent in regulating emerging technology. Many countries have already introduced regulatory frameworks for AI, including the European Union (EU), South Korea, Brazil, and Singapore.[54]

The EU passed the Artificial Intelligence Act[55] in 2023, implemented in August 2024, to address the risks to the environment, public health, and fundamental rights. While the AI Act does not impose direct statutory limits on carbon emissions, water usage, and e-waste generation, it establishes a baseline for transparency and accountability. As of July 2026, several major AI developers have signed the General-Purpose AI Code of Practice as part of this legislation, although Meta remains a notable exception.[56]

These instruments are critical, but they remain insufficient. Future legislation must build on this framework of safeguarding fundamental human rights and extend these protections to the environment. For instance, in March 2026, a bill introduced in the US Senate[57] proposed a moratorium on building new data centres until serious environmental concerns are addressed. The bill further sought to impose an export ban on computing hardware, such as chips and specialised processors, highlighting the need to prioritise finite resources. While a complete moratorium may not be achievable, regulatory interventions must ensure that AI serves environmental preservation rather than degradation. To this end, governments should mandate lifecycle environmental disclosures—covering training and inference energy, embodied carbon, resource usage, and water consumption—as a precondition for public procurement.
• Condition large-scale model training and data centre construction on prior adoption of sustainable cooling technologies and additionality-based renewable energy procurement.
• Deploy non-market instruments, including technology standards, R&D mandates, and green industrial policy, to drive abatement in AI infrastructure ahead of market correction.
• Introduce tiered water pricing for data centre operators, with higher surcharges in water-stressed catchments and revenues ringfenced for watershed restoration.
• Develop a multilateral siting framework weighted by renewable availability, water scarcity, and grid decarbonisation trajectory, prohibiting greenfield development in high-stress areas.

• Standardise sustainable cooling for data centres through regulatory mandates and environmental performance standards. This should include the adoption of closed-loop cooling systems that minimise freshwater losses through continuous recirculation, renewable-energy-powered air-cooling systems, and geothermal cooling solutions that leverage naturally lower underground temperatures to reduce cooling intensity and resource consumption.
• Mandate “community benefit agreements” covering compensation for land, grid strain, and water use, with required consultation with Indigenous and rural communities prior to siting approvals.

[d] Creative carbon accounting refers to the deliberate use of emissions accounting techniques to alter the actual level of carbon or environmental footprint of a firm in a way that benefits the management or other stakeholders, without necessarily violating accounting standards.
